hints: Notice the voltmeter is across only the variable resistor, so $V$ is the terminal p.d., while the $0.50\,\Omega$ internal resistance is inside the cell.
Recall $E = V + Ir$ for this loop, so $V = 3.0\,\text{V} - (0.50\,\Omega)I$ is a straight line with negative gradient.
Check the two ends: $I=0$ when the variable resistor is very large, and $V=0$ when it is shorted so $I = E/r$.
walkthrough: The voltmeter reads the p.d. across the external variable resistor, which is the terminal p.d. of the cell. The ammeter reads the loop current $I$.
Apply conservation of energy around the loop: $E = V + Ir$, so $V = E - Ir$.
Substitute $E = 3.0\,\text{V}$ and $r = 0.50\,\Omega$: $V = 3.0 - 0.50I$ with $V$ in $\text{V}$ and $I$ in $\text{A}$.
When $I = 0$, $V = 3.0\,\text{V}$. This is the $V$-intercept. When $V = 0$, $0 = 3.0 - 0.50I$ so $I = 3.0/0.50 = 6.0\,\text{A}$. This is the $I$-intercept.
The graph is therefore a straight line falling from $3.0\,\text{V}$ on the $V$-axis to $6.0\,\text{A}$ on the $I$-axis. This is option C.

A.explanation: V-intercept of $0.50\,\text{V}$ confuses internal resistance with e.m.f. The open-circuit terminal p.d. equals $E = 3.0\,\text{V}$.

B.explanation: I-intercept of $0.5\,\text{A}$ is wrong. Short-circuit current is $E/r = 6.0\,\text{A}$, not $0.5\,\text{A}$.

D.explanation: V-intercept of $6.0\,\text{V}$ is double the e.m.f. and I-intercept of $3.0\,\text{A}$ does not satisfy $I = E/r$.
